section: Chapter One — Dealings Before Idolater Festivals
subtitle: Prohibited commerce with idolaters in the three days before their festivals, and the rationale
author: Moses Maimonides
intro: Rambam's commentary on Tractate Avodah Zarah — the laws of idolatry, forbidden commercial dealings, libation wine, and the nullification of idols. Original 12th-century Judeo-Arabic with English translation.

aligned.ja: משנה [א]
aligned.en: Mishnah [1]

aligned.ja: אידיהן, חזנהם, כנאיה ען אעיאדהם, לם יסתחל אן יסמיהא אעיאד לאנהא אחזאן פי אלחקיקה. והד'ה אלת'אלת' איאם גיר יום אלעיד נפסה.
aligned.en: *Eideihen* — their festivals[^1] — is a periphrasis for *mo'adeihem*, their appointed times, because the mishnah refuses to call them festivals outright; in truth they are occasions of grief.[^2] The three days mentioned are the three days *before* the festival itself, not including the festival day.

pairs.en: is a periphrasis for *mo'adeihem*
occasions of grief
The three days mentioned
not including the festival day

fn.1: *Eideihen* (Heb. אידיהן) is an Aramaic form of the plural construct of *ed* (festival). The mishnah uses this Aramaic spelling, which Rambam notes is also a wordplay — *eid* can also mean "calamity" — allowing the Sages to avoid calling idolater observances by the honorific *ḥag* or *mo'ed*.
fn.2: Rambam explains the periphrastic choice as a normative act of linguistic distancing: calling pagan festivals "occasions of grief" encodes the rabbinic theological rejection of their legitimacy.

aligned.ja: וחרמנא אן ישאל מהן או ילוה מהן לאנהם ישכרון מעאבדהם עלי ד'לך פיכון אלסבב פי שכר עבודה זרה. ואן כאנת מלוה על פה פג'איז אכ'ד'הא לאנה מציל מידם.
aligned.en: The reason we are prohibited from extending a loan to idolaters during this period, or from accepting a loan from them, is that they will give thanks to their idols on account of that transaction, and one thereby becomes a contributing cause to the thanking of an idol.[^3] If, however, the loan is *be-al peh* — an oral loan, not secured by a written bond — it is permitted to collect it from them, because in doing so one is merely rescuing property from their hands.[^4]

pairs.ja: חרמנא אן ישאל מהן או ילוה מהן
pairs.en: prohibited from extending a loan to idolaters during this period, or from accepting a loan from them
they will give thanks to their idols
an oral loan, not secured by a written bond
rescuing property from their hands

fn.3: This is the core rationale Rambam gives throughout Ch. 1: the fear (*ḥashash*) that commercial profit will be dedicated as a thank-offering to the idol, making the Jew an indirect benefactor of idolatrous worship.
fn.4: A verbal, unwritten loan (*malveh be-al peh*) carries no document that the creditor can bring to court; collecting it therefore involves no new transaction and no fresh occasion for thanksgiving.

aligned.ja: ואין הלכה כר' יהודה.
aligned.en: The law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah.[^5]

pairs.en: The law does not follow
Rabbi Yehudah

fn.5: In the corresponding Mishnah, R. Yehudah extends the prohibition to written bonds even for collection; Rambam rejects this stringency.

aligned.ja: משנה [ב]
aligned.en: Mishnah [2]

aligned.ja: קטוע אלהלכה בגולה אין אסור אלא יום אידיהן פקט. וכל מא יבאע וישתרי מנהם פי יום עידהם אסור, אעני אן לא יג'וז אלאסתנפע בה.
aligned.en: The settled law in the Diaspora is that the prohibition applies only on the festival day itself.[^6] Anything sold to or purchased from them on that day is forbidden — meaning, one may derive no benefit whatsoever from it.

pairs.en: The settled law in the Diaspora

pairs.ja: אין אסור אלא יום אידיהן פקט
pairs.en: the prohibition applies only on the festival day itself
Anything sold to or purchased from them
one may derive no benefit whatsoever from it

fn.6: The Diaspora leniency (*Golah* ruling) reflects the practical reality that Jews in exile are surrounded by non-Jews and economic relations cannot be suspended for multiple days. On the festival day itself, however, the prohibition remains in full force.

aligned.ja: ואין הלכה כר' ישמעאל.
aligned.en: The law does not follow Rabbi Yishmael.

pairs.en: The law does not follow
Rabbi Yishmael

aligned.ja: משנה [ג]
aligned.en: Mishnah [3]

aligned.ja: הד'ה אלאעיאד אלמד'כורה כאנת משהורה פי ד'לך אלזמאן ענד אלנצארי ואלמנצ'אפין אליהם. וכד'לך כל מוסם ענד ג'מיע אלמלל פי ג'מיע אקטאר אלארץ' אד'א כאנוא עובדי עבודה זרה ילזם פיהא מא ד'כר.
aligned.en: The festivals enumerated in the mishnah were well known in that era among the Christians and those affiliated with them.[^7] Similarly, any seasonal festival (*mawsim*) observed by any community anywhere in the world, so long as its adherents are worshippers of idolatry, carries with it all the restrictions enumerated here.

pairs.en: The festivals enumerated in the mishnah
among the Christians and those affiliated with them
any seasonal festival (*mawsim*) observed by any community anywhere in the world
worshippers of idolatry

fn.7: Rambam refers to the specific Roman and Christian festival calendar known to the Tannaim and Amoraim: *Kalenda* (New Year), *Saturnalia*, *Kratesis*, and others listed in the Mishnah *(M. AZ 1:3)*.

aligned.ja: ואעלם אן הד'ה אלמלה אלנצראניה אלקאימה בדעוהֵ אלמסיח עלי אכתלאף פרקהא כלהם עובדי עבודה זרה ואידיהן כלהא חראם, וינהג' מעהם פי ג'מיע אלשריעה מא ינהג' מע עובדי עבודה זרה, ויום אלאחד הו מן ג'מלהֵ אידיהן של גוים. פלד'לך לא תג'וז מעאמלהֵ מעתקד אלמסיח פי יום אלאחד ראסא פי שי מן אלאשיא, בל ינהג' מעהם יום אלאחד מא ינהג' מע עובדי עבודה זרה פי יום אידן, וכד'א בין אלתלמוד.
aligned.en: Know, moreover, that the Christian community (*ha-millah ha-noẓranit*)[^8] — all of whose sects, for all their differences, claim to follow the Messiah — are idolaters in their entirety, and all their festivals are forbidden.[^9] One applies to them in every matter of religious law exactly what one applies to idol-worshippers. Sunday is among the festivals of the Gentiles;[^10] accordingly, commercial dealings with a Christian on Sunday are prohibited without exception, in any matter whatsoever. One treats Sunday for Christians exactly as one treats the day of an idolater's festival — and this is made clear in the Talmud *(BT AZ 2a)*.

pairs.en: the Christian community

pairs.ja: כלהם עובדי עבודה זרה ואידיהן כלהא חראם
pairs.en: are idolaters in their entirety, and all their festivals are forbidden

pairs.ja: יום אלאחד הו מן ג'מלהֵ אידיהן של גוים
pairs.en: Sunday is among the festivals of the Gentiles

pairs.ja: לא תג'וז מעאמלהֵ מעתקד אלמסיח פי יום אלאחד
pairs.en: commercial dealings with a Christian on Sunday are prohibited without exception
this is made clear in the Talmud

fn.8: *Ha-millah ha-noẓranit* — literally "the Christian community/nation." Rambam treats Christianity as a legally unified category regardless of sectarian divisions, because all its sects maintain some form of devotional practice directed at a human figure (Jesus), which he classifies as idolatry.
fn.9: This is one of Rambam's most explicit statements on the legal status of Christians vis-à-vis idolatry. He does not qualify it with reference to trinitarian vs. unitarian variants; all sects fall under the same ruling.
fn.10: Sunday (*yom ha-aḥad*) is the weekly festival of Christians. Rambam extends the Mishnah's three-day prohibition to the period preceding each Sunday, not merely to annual festivals — a significant halakhic stringency in daily life.

aligned.ja: מיתה שיש בה שריפה, יכון פיהא בכ'ור או חריק ת'יאב אלמית ואואניה. וגניסיה של מלכים, הו אן יג'תמעון פיה ליקדמוא מלך.
aligned.en:
*Mitah sheyesh bah serefah* — a death that involves burning — means that the body of the deceased, along with his vessels and garments, is burned.[^11]

*Genisiyah shel melakhim* — the royal assembly[^12] — is a gathering convened to honor the king.

pairs.en: a death that involves burning
his vessels and garments, is burned
the royal assembly
a gathering convened to honor the king

fn.11: *Mitah sheyesh bah serefah* — a mode of death (execution or natural death?) associated with burning. Rambam clarifies it as a type of pagan funerary custom in which the body along with its belongings is cremated.
fn.12: *Genisiyah shel melakhim* — a royal coronation assembly (*genisiyah* from Gk. *genesion*, birthday or accession celebration). Non-Jews gather to honor the king with quasi-religious ceremonial, rendering attendance at such a gathering prohibited.

aligned.ja: ואין הלכה כר' מאיר. ובלורית, הו אלשער אלד'י יתרך פי וסט אלראס ויחלק מא דאר בה מן אלג'האת כלהא. והד'א אלנחו מן אלחלאק חראם פי שריעתנא איצ'א ללא נתשבה בהם, לכן לא ילזם פיה מלקות אלא אן חלק אלפאות כמא בינא פי מכות.
aligned.en:
The law does not follow Rabbi Meir.

*Bulyarit* — a lock of hair left at the center of the head while the surrounding hair is shaved away on all sides.[^13] This style of cutting is likewise forbidden by our law, lest we imitate their practice. However, lashes are not incurred for it unless one also shaves the *pe'ot* (sidelocks), as we explained in tractate *Makkot*.

pairs.en: *Bulyarit*

pairs.ja: שער אלד'י יתרך פי וסט אלראס
pairs.en: a lock of hair left at the center of the head

pairs.ja: ויחלק מא דאר בה מן אלג'האת כלהא
pairs.en: the surrounding hair is shaved away on all sides

pairs.ja: אלנחו מן אלחלאק חראם פי שריעתנא איצ'א ללא נתשבה בהם
pairs.en: likewise forbidden by our law, lest we imitate their practice

pairs.ja: לא ילזם פיה מלקות אלא אן חלק אלפאות
pairs.en: lashes are not incurred for it unless one also shaves the *pe'ot*

fn.13: *Bulyarit* — likely the Roman *cirrus* or "forelock" style: a tuft left at the crown while all surrounding hair is closely cropped. Rambam connects it to the prohibition on imitating idolater customs (*lo telkhu be-ḥuqqoteihem*, Lev 18:3), but distinguishes it from the Biblical prohibition on rounding the *pe'ot* (Lev 19:27), for which lashes are incurred.

aligned.ja: משנה [ד]
aligned.en: Mishnah [4]

aligned.ja: קולה מה הוא לילך לשם, אן יג'עלהא טריק לימשי מנהא לגירהא, לאן לא יחל בוג'ה דכ'ול מדינה יכון פיהא עבודה זרה, פנאהיך ען סכנאהא, פנאהיך ען אלתג'ר פיהא. וחניות מעוטרות, אלחואנת אלמזינה באי נוע מן אלזינה פהי אנמא זינת לעבודה זרה, ולד'לך כל מא פיהא אסור בהניה.
aligned.en:
His statement *mah hu le-lekh le-sham* — "what about going there" — means: making the city a route through which one passes on the way to somewhere else. For it is absolutely forbidden to enter a city that contains an idol — still less to reside there, and still less to conduct commerce there.[^14]

*Ḥanuyot me'uvarot* — shops adorned [in honor of the festival]: any shop decorated in any manner has been adorned for the sake of idolatry, and therefore everything in it is forbidden for benefit (*assur be-hana'ah*).[^15]

pairs.en: *mah hu le-lekh le-sham*

pairs.ja: לא יחל בוג'ה דכ'ול מדינה יכון פיהא עבודה זרה
pairs.en: absolutely forbidden to enter a city that contains an idol
*Ḥanuyot me'uvarot* — shops adorned
everything in it is forbidden for benefit

fn.14: Rambam derives a hierarchy of prohibitions: passing through (using as a route) → residing → conducting commerce. Even the most minimal engagement — making the idolatrous city a waypoint on a journey — is forbidden in principle.
fn.15: *Assur be-hana'ah* — forbidden for any benefit or use, not merely for consumption. This is the stronger form of prohibition, equivalent to the status of libation wine (*yayin nesekh*), meaning one may not sell the prohibited item to recover its value.

aligned.ja: ולד'לך יעלם אן כל בלד מן בלאד אלמלה אלנצראניה יכון להם פיה במה אעני בית מצלאהם אלד'י הו בית עבודה זרה בלא שך, פאן ד'לך אלבלד לא יג'וז אלעבור עליה באלקצד פכיף סכנאה. לכן אללה תלנא באידיהם חתי נסכן בלאדהם באלקהר לית'בת ועידה ועבדתם שם אלהים מעשה ידי אדם עץ ואבן.
aligned.en: From this one should understand that any city of Christendom that contains a church — which is unquestionably a house of idol-worship — may not even be passed through intentionally, let alone inhabited. But God has placed us in their hands until we dwell in their cities under compulsion, fulfilling the verse *"And there you shall serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone"* *(Deut 4:28)*.

pairs.ja: כל בלד מן בלאד אלמלה אלנצראניה
pairs.en: any city of Christendom
unquestionably a house of idol-worship
may not even be passed through intentionally

pairs.ja: תלנא באידיהם חתי נסכן בלאדהם באלקהר
pairs.en: God has placed us in their hands until we dwell in their cities under compulsion

aligned.ja: ואד'א כאן הד'א חכם אלבלד נאהיך ען חכם בית עבודה זרה נפסה לאנה יחרם נט'רה יכאד, פכיף אלקרב מנה, פכיף דכ'ולה.
aligned.en: If this is the ruling for the city itself, how much more so for the house of worship itself — for even glancing at it is almost forbidden; proximity to it is worse still; entering it is worst of all.

pairs.en: the ruling for the city itself
the house of worship itself
even glancing at it is almost forbidden
entering it is worst of all

aligned.ja: משנה [ה]
aligned.en: Mishnah [5]

aligned.ja: אצטרובילין, אלצנובר אלצגיר אלד'י יסמי קצ'ם קריש. ובנות שוח, נוע מן אלג'מיז. ופטוטרותיהן, אטראפהא אלתי תתעלק בהא מן אלשג'רה.
aligned.en:
*Ishtrovilin* — the small pine nut known as *qadam quraysh*.[^16]

*Benot shuaḥ* — a variety of fig.

*Petotroteḥen* — the tips that hang from the tree by which they are attached to the branch.

pairs.en: *Ishtrovilin*
the small pine nut
*Benot shuaḥ*
*Petotroteḥen*

pairs.ja: אטראפהא אלתי תתעלק בהא מן אלשג'רה
pairs.en: the tips that hang from the tree by which they are attached to the branch

fn.16: *Ishtrovilin* — likely the stone pine (*Pinus pinea*) or a related species; Rambam glosses it with the local Arabic name *qadam quraysh* (lit. "Quraysh foot"), evidently a regional colloquialism for a small pine nut.

aligned.ja: וקול ר' מאיר דקל טב, יריד בה פירות דקל טב, לאן אלפאכהה אלטיבה יקדמונהא לעבודה זרה. וחצב, קצב אלסכר. ונקליבס, נוע מן אלחשאיש רפיע איצ'א.
aligned.en:
Rabbi Meir's mention of *tamar tov* — fine dates — means the fruit of a superior palm, since choice fruit is offered before the idol.

*Ḥaẓav* — sugar cane.

*Naqlibis* — another species of refined vegetation.

pairs.en: *tamar tov* — fine dates
choice fruit is offered before the idol
*Ḥaẓav* — sugar cane
*Naqlibis*

aligned.ja: וקול ר' יהודה אנה אין מקריבין חסר לעבודה זרה, צחיח, וכד'לך הלכה כר' מאיר אלד'י יחרם ביע הד'ה אלאשיא גזרה שמא יקריב מהם לעבודה זרה.
aligned.en: Rabbi Yehudah's ruling that one does not offer a deficient thing before idolatry is correct.[^17] And so too the law follows Rabbi Meir, who forbids the sale of these items as a preventive decree, lest any of them be offered to an idol.

pairs.en: one does not offer a deficient thing before idolatry
the law follows Rabbi Meir
forbids the sale of these items

pairs.ja: גזרה שמא יקריב מהם לעבודה זרה
pairs.en: a preventive decree, lest any of them be offered to an idol

fn.17: This parenthetical endorsement of R. Yehudah's principle — that blemished or incomplete items are not brought as idol-offerings — serves as the theoretical underpinning of R. Meir's restrictive ruling: *because* only fine produce is used for idol offerings, fine produce is precisely what must not be sold near festival time.

aligned.ja: משנה [ו]
aligned.en: Mishnah [6]

aligned.ja: בהמה גסה חרם ביעהא לגוי לאנה מצווה על שביתת בהמתו, פחרס ביעהא מנה עלי ג'ההֵ אלגזרה איאך יעירהא מן גוי או יכריהא מנה, ויקול כמא יג'וז ביעהא יג'וז כראהא ועאריתהא, ויכ'דמהא אלגוי והי של ישראל, ולד'לך יג'וז לה ביעהא עלי ידי סמסאר כמא בינא פי אלראבע מן פסחים.
aligned.en: Large cattle (*behemah gasah*) are forbidden to be sold to a non-Jew because a Jew is commanded concerning the rest of his animal *(Exod 20:10)*; it is therefore forbidden to transfer the animal to a non-Jew who is under no such obligation. This is a Rabbinic decree.[^18] Similarly, one may not lease cattle to a non-Jew or lend it to him, claiming that just as selling is permitted in certain circumstances so too leasing ought to be — for the non-Jew will use the animal and put it to labor. Nevertheless, one may sell such an animal through an intermediary broker, as we explained in the fourth chapter of *Pesaḥim* *(M. Pes. 4)*.

pairs.en: Large cattle (*behemah gasah*) are forbidden to be sold to a non-Jew
a Jew is commanded concerning the rest of his animal
This is a Rabbinic decree
sell such an animal through an intermediary broker

fn.18: The prohibition on selling large cattle to non-Jews is Rabbinic (*de-rabbanan*), not Biblical. The Biblical commandment of Sabbath rest for one's animals (Exod 20:10, Deut 5:14) applies only so long as the animal is under the Jew's ownership; the Rabbinic fence prevents circumventing the spirit of that commandment by transferring ownership.

aligned.ja: ואלשבורה איצ'א קד תכ'דם פי אלטואחן, ובן בתירה יקול אלכ'יל אלתי ינקל עליהא אלציאדון טיור אלציד יג'וז ביעהא מנהם, לאנה יעתקד החי נושא את עצמו ואפילו בהמה ועוף כמא בינא פי ראבע פסחים. ואלחכמים יקולון אן אדם פקט הו אלד'י נקול פיה החי נושא את עצמו כמא תבין פי אלעאשר מן שבת.
aligned.en: An animal that is lame (*ha-shevurah*) may also be put to work at a mill. Ben Beteira holds that horses used by hunters to transport game birds may be sold to them, because he maintains the principle "a living creature carries itself" (*ha-ḥay nosei et aẓmo*) — even animals and fowl — as we explained in the fourth chapter of *Pesaḥim*. The Sages, however, hold that this principle applies only to a human being, as is clarified in the tenth chapter of *Shabbat* *(BT Shab. 94a)*.[^19]

pairs.en: An animal that is lame

pairs.ja: אלכ'יל אלתי ינקל עליהא אלציאדון טיור אלציד
pairs.en: horses used by hunters to transport game birds
a living creature carries itself

pairs.ja: אדם פקט הו אלד'י נקול פיה
pairs.en: this principle applies only to a human being

fn.19: The Talmudic principle *ha-ḥay nosei et aẓmo* (a living creature supports its own weight) was invoked to argue that carrying an animal does not constitute "carrying a burden" on the Sabbath, and by extension that selling a horse whose burden is itself (as it carries the hunter) is unobjectionable. The Sages limit this principle to humans.

aligned.ja: ואין הלכה כבן בתירה. ואין הלכה כר' יהודה. פאמא סאיר אלכ'יל פיג'וז ביעהא מן גוי לאן מעלומהא אן ירכבהא אלאנסאן פקט.
aligned.en:
The law does not follow Ben Beteira. The law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah.

As for other horses, it is permitted to sell them to a non-Jew, since it is well known that their ordinary use is for riding only.

pairs.en: The law does not follow Ben Beteira
The law does not follow Rabbi Yehudah

pairs.ja: סאיר אלכ'יל פיג'וז ביעהא מן גוי
pairs.en: other horses, it is permitted to sell them to a non-Jew
their ordinary use is for riding only

aligned.ja: משנה [ז]
aligned.en: Mishnah [7]

aligned.ja: כל דבר שיש בו ניזקה לרבים, מת'ל אלאת אלחרב כלהא ואלאת אלעד'אב נחו אלסלאסל ואלכבול ואלאגלאל, וכד'לך לא תצלח להם אלאת אלחרב ולא תסקל להם אלסיוף ואלרמאח ונחוהא, ללא יעאן אלמפסדין פי אלארץ' עלי אלפסאד.
aligned.en: Everything that poses a danger to the public (*kol davar sheyesh bo nizkah le-rabbim*) — such as all weapons of war and instruments of torture, including chains, fetters, and shackles — is likewise forbidden to sharpen for them or to sell to them. One does not polish swords or spears or the like for them, so as not to assist those who spread violence throughout the land.[^20]

pairs.ja: כל דבר שיש בו ניזקה לרבים
pairs.en: Everything that poses a danger to the public
all weapons of war and instruments of torture
chains, fetters, and shackles
One does not polish swords or spears

pairs.ja: ללא יעאן אלמפסדין פי אלארץ' עלי אלפסאד
pairs.en: so as not to assist those who spread violence throughout the land

fn.20: Rambam frames this prohibition in universal ethical terms — "assisting those who corrupt the earth" (*ma'azerim al ha-fasad*) — not merely as a particularist Jewish concern. This is characteristic of his rationalist jurisprudence, grounding specific laws in general moral principles.

fn.21: *Basilki* (Gk. *basilike*, royal hall), *girdon* (Lat. *circus*?), *istadya* (Gk. *stadion*), and *bimah* — all are public spaces of assembly where idol-worship, games, or judicial spectacles with idolatrous dimensions took place. Rambam reads them as platforms (*manābir wa-manāṣib*) erected in honor of idolatry.
fn.22: Rambam's gloss of *bimosot* as *qaṣūr* is opaque; the word may mean "abbreviated" or may indicate a damaged manuscript reading. The term *bimos* (from Gk. *bōmos*) elsewhere in rabbinic literature denotes a stone idol-plinth or sacrificial altar.

aligned.ja: אצל תחרים הד'ה אלאשיא קולה תעלי לא תחנם, ג'א אלנקל לא תתן להם חניה בקרקע לאן ד'לך דאכ'ל תחת לא תחנם. וקולה ואין צריך לומר שדות, לאן אלשדות פיהא קצתאן, ואחדה מן עלהֵ לא תחנם, ות'אניה אנה יעטל מנהא אכ'ראג' אלתרומה ואלמעשרות.
aligned.en: The Scriptural basis for these prohibitions is the verse *"You shall not give them a foothold"* (*lo teḥannem*, Deut 7:2) — from which tradition derives: do not grant them lodging (*ḥanayah*) in the land, since that falls under the prohibition of *lo teḥannem*.[^23] As for the statement "it goes without saying regarding fields" — fields carry two prohibitions: the first under *lo teḥannem*, and the second because withholding them prevents the separation of *terumah* and *ma'asrot*.[^24]

pairs.en: The Scriptural basis for these prohibitions
*lo teḥannem*

fn.23: *Lo teḥannem* (Deut 7:2) — "you shall not show them favor." The midrashic-halakhic reading splits the word into *lo titten lahem ḥanayah ba-qarqa'* — do not grant them lodging in the land — yielding a prohibition on transferring real property to non-Jews in the Land of Israel. Rambam cites this as the Biblical foundation for the restrictions in this mishnah.
fn.24: *Terumah* and *ma'asrot* — priestly tithe and Levitical tithe. Agricultural land in non-Jewish hands generates no obligation to separate these sacred portions; selling such land to non-Jews therefore removes sanctified agricultural obligations from those fields, compounding the Biblical prohibition.

aligned.ja: והלכה כר' יוסי. ובשרט אן יכרי לשכ'ץ או את'נין, אמא ת'לאת'ה פמא זאד פלא יכרי להם שיא שלא יעשם שכונת גוים.
aligned.en: The law follows Rabbi Yossi. The condition is that one may rent to one or two individuals, but not to three or more, lest this constitute the establishment of an idolater's neighborhood (*shekhunath goyim*).[^25]

fn.25: Three or more non-Jewish residents in proximity constitute, by rabbinic definition, a neighborhood (*shekhunah*) with its attendant social pressures and risks of assimilation. The numerical threshold is halakhic, not merely demographic.

aligned.ja: קולה אף במקום שאמרו להשכיר, הו כלאם ר' מאיר אלד'י יקול לא יכרי מנהם גיר פי סוריה פקט לא פי ארץ ישראל. אמא עלי מד'הב ר' יוסי פיכון נסק אלכלאם וכשאמרו להשכיר לא לבית דירה אמרו. ולא כ'לאף פי ד'לך אנה אנמא יכרי מנה בית ליתכ'ד'ה מכ'זן או ליסתעין בה מעונה יסירה עלי גההֵ אלערץ' ותג'ויז אלוקת.
aligned.en: The statement *"even where they said it is permitted to rent"* is Rabbi Meir's view, which holds that renting is permitted only in Syria, not in the Land of Israel. According to Rabbi Yossi's view, the clause reads coherently: "and where they permitted renting, they permitted it only for use as a storehouse, not as a residence."[^26] There is no dispute on this point — one may rent to a non-Jew only for use as a warehouse, or for very limited and incidental residence on a temporary or makeshift basis.

pairs.en: *"even where they said it is permitted to rent"*

fn.26: The dispute between R. Meir and R. Yossi concerns the geographical and functional scope of the rental permission. R. Meir (stricter) allows rental only in Syria (a borderland with an intermediate status between the Land of Israel and the Diaspora); R. Yossi (more lenient within Israel itself) allows rental for storage but not for residence.

aligned.ja: וקולה על שמו, יעני על שם ישראל בעל המרחץ, ואלגוי אלד'י יכריה יסכ'נה פי אלסבת ויכ'דמהא אלגוים ויקולון נחם פי חמאם פלאן אליום, ופי ד'לך חלול השם למן יסמע ד'לך ולא יעלם אנה מכרי בידה למדה מקטועה בת'מן מעין.
aligned.en: His statement *"al shemo"* — "in his name" — means: in the name of the Israelite who owns the bathhouse. The non-Jew who rents it will operate it on the Sabbath and admit non-Jewish bathers, who will say, "Let us bathe at so-and-so's bathhouse today." This constitutes a desecration of God's name (*ḥillul ha-Shem*) in the ears of anyone who hears it without knowing that it has been rented out for a fixed fee.[^27]

fn.27: The concern is *ḥillul ha-Shem* — desecration of God's name — through the public perception that a Jewish-owned establishment operates on the Sabbath under the Jew's direction. Rambam emphasizes that this concern was era-specific: in his own day, rental arrangements were universally understood to transfer operating control, eliminating the appearance problem.

aligned.ja: והד'א כאן פי זמאנהם אלתי כאנת אלעאדה ענדהם כמא ד'כרוא אריסותא למרחץ לא עבדי אנשי, אמא פי זמאננא הד'א פחכם אלמרחץ ואלפדן וסאיר אלאמלאך סוי, לאן רב כל מלך יכריה, והד'א משהור ענד אלנאס אג'מע.
aligned.en: This ruling applied in their time, when the practice was the lease arrangement for a bathhouse described as *aristuta le-merḥaẓ* — a lump-sum rental that did not involve the labor of the owner's servants. In our own era, however, the rule governing a bathhouse, a farm (*fadan*), and all other properties is the same: since it is standard practice for every estate-owner to rent out his property, and this is universally well known, there is no concern for the appearance of impropriety.
